title: Throttled streaming + KV reservation windows with heterogeneous model fallback
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a low-latency, memory-aware mitigation path for out-of-memory (OOM) events that combines small per-request KV reservation windows, throttled streaming/backoff, and a deterministic heterogeneous-model fallback chain. Motivation: we continue to see tail OOMs under mixed workloads when large-context streaming requests coincide with heavy KV cache pressure and large batch assembly. Existing soft-eviction flows are reactive and cause hard failures for high-priority requests (retries, customer-visible 5xx).

Scope:
- Add per-request KV reservation windows: requests may reserve a small guaranteed KV quota (in number of KV entries and bytes) for the lifetime of the generation. Reservation is supplied by scheduler at enqueue time and honored during continuous-batching assembly.
- Throttled streaming/backoff: when reservation can't be satisfied immediately, allow the request to enter a throttled streaming mode (smaller step allocations, earlier partial flushes) rather than full abort. This keeps tail latency bounded while reducing peak memory pressure.
- Heterogeneous model fallback chain: define an ordered list of compatible fallback variants (same model quantized variant -> smaller-context model -> short-context distilled model) with deterministic costs and quality trade-offs. Fallbacks happen only after graceful throttled retries and KV-trim attempts.
- Integrations: scheduler, batch assembler, KV manager, and serving runtime must exchange reservation metadata and fallback hints.

Success criteria:
- Reduce customer-facing OOM-induced 5xx by 80% for mixed streaming workloads in staging.
- 95th percentile latency increase <= 30% for requests that enter throttled mode.
- Automated Canary rollout with telemetry (OOM events, fallback rate, quality degradation score).

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Reservation granularity: we chose KV entry counts + byte-estimates rather than per-token reservations to avoid tight coupling to tokenizer variations. This simplifies byte accounting across tokenizers but requires conservative headroom.
- Reservation vs. admission control: admitting fewer requests up-front improves stability but harms throughput. Our path favors admitting and throttling (degrade-instead-of-block) for customer-facing low-latency routes, while administrative routes may choose strict admission control.
- Fallback ordering: prioritize quantized variants before switching models to preserve output semantics. If quantized variant is unavailable, the scheduler will try smaller-context models but preserves prefix context where possible via partial KV snapshotting.

Files and artifacts:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUN/kv-reservation-throttled-fallback
- Implementation spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4921
- Canary dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/oom-mitigation/kv-reservation-canary

Open questions:
- Should reservation accounting include ephemeral transient objects (e.g., attention buffers during cross-attention) or only persistent KV bytes? We opted to start with persistent KV bytes and measure.
- How aggressively should we trim KV entries for throttled requests vs. evicting less-recent entries globally? Policy tuning will be empirical.

Planned milestones:
1) Spike: runtime hooks + KV reservation metadata (done)
2) Scheduler adapter + throttled streaming shim (in PR)
3) Fallback policy config + deterministic chain executor (staging canary)
4) Telemetry + automated rollback triggers (canary -> gradual rollout)
